title: Classical simulation and model concentration in passive linear optics
authors: Léo Monbroussou, Hugo Thomas, Hela Mhiri, Zoë Holmes, Elham Kashefi
abstract: Passive linear optics is a restricted model of quantum computation, with complexity-theoretic evidence of quantum advantage for sampling tasks and low losses that make it attractive for near-term algorithms. In qubit architectures, a body of work has revealed a close connection between barren plateaus and classical simulability. Whether an analogous tradeoff exists for bosonic systems remains largely unexplored. Building on a recently developed representation-theoretic framework for moments of random passive linear-optical circuits, we characterize the concentration of expectation values for relevant families of particle-number-preserving observables by evaluating their projections into irreducible representations of the unitary group and analyzing their asymptotic scaling. We show that concentration is governed by the misalignment of the projections into irreducible representations of the input state and the observable, giving a unified representation-theoretic interpretation of generalized entanglement and locality in the bosonic setting. We further relate these concentration properties to existing classical simulation techniques, identifying broad classes of trainable observables that admit efficient classical simulation. Conversely, we identify Fock-state inputs and observables that appear to evade exponential concentration while retaining a polynomially large signal component not accessible to known efficient classical simulation methods. The separation is only partial: most of the signal remains classically tractable, and the residual part, while not exponentially suppressed, is small enough that a truncation serves as a classical surrogate with polynomially small error. Our framework nonetheless provides a systematic route for searching for regimes that unambiguously combine the absence of exponential concentration and lies beyond known efficient classical simulation methods.
summary: This work develops a representation-theoretic framework to study how expectation values behave in passive linear optics. By analyzing projections onto irreducible representations, the authors characterize when these systems exhibit exponential concentration or retain signals that are classically hard to simulate. This provides a systematic route for understanding quantum advantage in bosonic photonic circuits.
main_problem: The paper characterizes the concentration of expectation values for observables in passive linear optics, aiming to establish an analogous tradeoff between quantum advantage and classical simulability for bosonic systems.
main_result: Concentration is governed by the misalignment of projections into irreducible representations (irreps) of the unitary group. The authors identify regimes that evade exponential concentration while retaining a signal component not accessible to known efficient classical simulation methods.
method: The analysis employs a representation-theoretic framework, decomposing operators and states into irreps of $U(m)$ to calculate variances over random unitaries (Haar measure).
model_or_system: The system is passive linear optics, modeled by photon evolution through beam splitters and phase shifters, described by unitary transformations $U \in U(m)$ acting on fixed particle-number sectors $\mathcal{F}_n$.
key_observables: Expectation values of particle-number-preserving observables ($\langle \hat{O} angle$), generalized entanglement (state purity), and generalized locality (observable purity).
important_parameters: Photon number ($n$), number of modes ($m$), and the scaling index $k$ used for irrep decomposition.
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on fixed total photon numbers ($n$) and utilizes theorems derived from averaging over Haar-random unitaries. The separation between hard/easy regimes is noted to be only partial.
figures_summary: Figure 1 summarizes four regimes based on irrep decomposition (Exponential Concentration, No concentration/small irreps, etc.). Figure 2 shows the scaling of Fock-state purities for different choices of irrep indices $k$ relative to $n$.
paper_structure: The paper develops a representation-theoretic framework by decomposing operators into irreducible representations. It then applies this to calculate variances over random unitaries, relating concentration properties to entanglement/locality measures and comparing these findings against known classical simulation techniques for specific observables.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful mathematical tool (representation theory) to analyze the complexity of quantum optical circuits, directly linking physical diagnostics (concentration) to computational hardness.
